analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid to cover home-based attendant care so disabled and older people can live at home instead of nursing homes.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 125 cosponsors, including 28 Republicans, but never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicaid, the only long-term care service the federal government guarantees in every state is nursing home care. This bill would have added a second guarantee: if you need nursing-home-level care but choose to live at home, Medicaid would have to pay for an aide to help you there — bathing, dressing, meals, health tasks — under a plan you help direct, including paying a family member as the attendant. States that signed on early would get a bigger federal match to soften the cost, plus grants to build the home-care workforce. The bill sat in committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid-eligible people with disabilities and older Americans who need nursing-home-level care but want to live in their own homes and communities; their families, who could be paid as attendants instead of providing unpaid care; and home care workers, whose pay, training, and career prospects the bill funded states to improve.

how_it_helps.text: Makes community-based attendant services a mandatory Medicaid benefit for anyone who qualifies for nursing-home-level care and chooses to receive care at home, effective statewide and without regard to age or type of disability.

Offers states that adopt the benefit early an enhanced federal match, plus 10 extra percentage points on certain expenditures and federal payment of 70–90% on costs exceeding 150% of the average nursing home cost, to ease the transition.

Authorizes $50 million a year in grants for states to build community-based care systems, including seeding consumer-controlled cooperatives, small businesses, and worker training that enhances attendants' earnings and career prospects.
Allows qualified family members to serve as paid attendants and gives the individual — not an agency alone — the right to select, manage, and dismiss the provider of care.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state taxpayers through expanded Medicaid long-term care spending; the bill's own findings acknowledge the Medicaid program carries a heavy institutional bias that the shift would unwind over time, and home-based care can cost more than a nursing home for some individuals.

drawbacks.text: Adding a mandatory home-based benefit expands Medicaid spending for both the federal government and states, even with the enhanced federal match the bill offers to early-adopting states.

For some individuals, community-based care costs more than a nursing home — the bill sets its extra federal payment threshold at 150% of average nursing home cost, an acknowledgment that the cheapest option is not always community care.

Care delivered in scattered private homes is harder to monitor than care in facilities; the bill requires an extensive state quality-assurance system, mandatory abuse reporting, and provider sanctions precisely because of that oversight challenge.
The benefit would depend on a much larger paid attendant workforce; the bill funds recruitment and training but supply shortages could delay access in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people affected, the benefit is concrete and life-changing: instead of nursing home placement being the only federally guaranteed option, living at home with an aide becomes an equal choice. The cost is real money — a new mandatory Medicaid entitlement — and the bill leans on the argument in its own findings that community care is generally the more cost-effective alternative to institutional care, while the enhanced federal match and the 150% cost threshold are designed to keep state exposure manageable. An honest supporter would acknowledge the fiscal and workforce burden is significant even if the long-term direction saves money.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and then to its Health Subcommittee, and neither ever took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 21, 2007, by Rep. Danny Davis of Illinois, joined at introduction by Rep. John Shimkus, a Republican.
It gathered 125 cosponsors — 97 Democrats and 28 Republicans — showing support across both parties.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on March 21, 2007, and to that committee's Health Subcommittee the next day.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The institutional long-term care industry kept the status quo in which nursing home care is the only long-term care service federal law guarantees in every state, and people with disabilities and older Americans continued facing nursing home placement as their guaranteed default. State governments also avoided taking on a new mandatory benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home industry and the institutional status quo

for.name: Rep. John Shimkus
for.what_they_did: Joined the Democratic sponsor at introduction, giving the bill a Republican voice from day one.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup; no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The 125 cosponsors split 97 Democrats and 28 Republicans, and the bill's two introducers were one Democrat and one Republican; the opposition was not a recorded vote but the committee's decision never to act.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: Under current Medicaid law, nursing home care is the only long-term care service guaranteed in every state, which keeps a captive stream of public money flowing to these facilities; this bill would add an equally guaranteed home-based alternative that Medicaid recipients clearly prefer. The industry's interest in preserving the institutional-only guarantee ran directly against the choice the bill would have given disabled and older people.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and attendant service providers
industries.note: The bill would create a mandatory, statewide Medicaid payer for attendant services and fund $50 million a year in grants to expand capacity, including consumer-controlled cooperatives and small provider businesses. Home care workers' earnings and training were also funded priorities, so the industry's gain and the public's gain point the same way.

States would take on a mandatory new benefit, but the bill sweetens it with an enhanced federal match for early adopters, extra percentage points on certain expenditures, and up to 90% federal payment on high-cost cases above 150% of nursing home cost. Many states already spend heavily on institutional care they would partially convert.
